# 6. Drawing

The canvas `g` appears only as a parameter: the second parameter of `on_draw(ctx, g)`, and the parameter of `layer:draw(function(g) end)`. The canvas is valid only during that call. Using it afterwards makes every call return `nil, "inactive"`.

```lua
g:size()                                  -- width, height
g:clear(color)                            -- color defaults to 0
g:line(x0, y0, x1, y1, opts)
g:rect(x, y, w, h, opts)
g:circle(cx, cy, r, opts)
g:arc(cx, cy, r, start_deg, end_deg, opts)
g:polyline(points, opts)
g:polygon(points, opts)
g:pattern(x, y, w, h, opts)               -- optional capability pattern
g:text(x, y, text, opts)                  -- section 7
g:text_box(x, y, w, h, text, opts)        -- section 7
g:image(image, x, y, opts)
```

Success returns nothing.

## Style

| Field | Used by | Values | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `color` | all | 0..15 | 15 |
| `fill` | `rect` `circle` `polygon` | boolean | false, stroke only |
| `line_width` | strokes, `line`, `arc`, `polyline` | 1–255 | 1 |
| `radius` | `rect` | 0–255 | 0 |

`points` is a flat coordinate array `{ x1, y1, x2, y2, ... }`: `polyline` takes 2 to 128 points, `polygon` takes 3 to 128 points. The wrong count, or an odd length, returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. `r` is an integer from 0 to 32767. `start_deg` and `end_deg` are integer degrees. 0 degrees is due right, and clockwise is positive. When the two differ by an integer multiple of 360, nothing is drawn.

## Pixel rules

The center of pixel `(px, py)` is `(px + 0.5, py + 0.5)`.

| Call | Pixels covered |
| --- | --- |
| `rect` fill | `[x, x+w) × [y, y+h)`. Nothing is drawn when `w` or `h` is not greater than 0 |
| `rect` stroke | The band inside the filled area whose distance to the outer edge is less than `line_width`. It grows inward only |
| `rect` with `radius` | The four corners are clipped to a circle: row `dy` (counting from 0) insets by `r - round(sqrt(r^2 - (r - dy - 0.5)^2))`. A `radius` past half the short side is treated as half the short side |
| `circle` fill | Distance from the center to `(cx + 0.5, cy + 0.5)` is less than `r` |
| `circle` stroke | The filled area whose distance is not less than `r - line_width` |
| `arc` | The part of a `circle` stroke from `start_deg` clockwise to `end_deg` |
| `line` | When `line_width` is 1, Bresenham, and both ends are drawn. When thicker, pixels whose distance to the segment is less than `line_width / 2` |
| `polyline` | `line` between adjacent points, in order. An overlap is drawn once |
| `polygon` fill | Pixels whose center is inside the polygon, by the even-odd rule. The first and last points are closed automatically |
| `polygon` stroke | The same as `polyline`, plus the last point back to the first |

## Patterns

When `ctx.capabilities.pattern` is true, `g.pattern` exists. Otherwise it is nil. `opts.kind` is `dot`, `line`, or `cross`, default `dot`. `opts.density` is an integer from 0 to 100, default 50, the percentage of the area covered by ink. `opts.color` defaults to 15. A pattern is aligned to the canvas origin, so two adjacent blocks meet with no seam.

## Images

`image` is an object returned by `ctx.package:image` or `ctx.layers:create`. Any other value returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. An object that has been released returns `nil, "invalid_handle"`. Drawing a layer into itself returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`.

| Field | Values | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `w` `h` | 1–4096. Scaling happens only when both are set, with nearest-neighbor sampling | the image's own size |
| `color` | 0..15. Only for a black-and-white image: ink dots are drawn in this color (tint an icon) | 15 |
| `invert` | boolean | false |
| `background` | 0..15. When set, the destination rectangle is filled with it first, then the image is drawn | no fill |
| `radius` | 0–255, clips the output to rounded corners | 0 |
| `gray` | Boolean (2.11). true makes this frame a gray frame; see "Gray frames" in section 3 | false |

**Transparency comes from the asset itself**, the same way as PNG:

- The asset carries transparency (the PNG before packaging had an alpha channel): transparent pixels are not drawn, and what is already on the canvas stays. Opaque pixels are drawn as usual, and white is drawn as white.
- The asset carries no transparency: the whole image is opaque, and white covers whatever is underneath.
- A partly transparent pixel: on a device whose `gray_levels` is 2, opacity of at least 50% is drawn and less than that is not. A device with more gray levels uses the same 50% test. There is no blending.

Per pixel: look at transparency first. An opaque pixel takes the source color (an ink dot of a black-and-white image is `color`, a paper dot is 0; a grayscale image uses its own color). `invert` takes `15 - color`, then the gray-level mapping in section 3 is applied. `invert` does not change transparency.

When `ctx.capabilities.image_transform` is true, `flip_x` and `flip_y` (booleans), `rotate` (integer degrees, clockwise, modulo 360), `pivot_x`, and `pivot_y` (relative to the top left of the destination rectangle, default the rectangle's center) may also be set. The order is scale, flip, rotate, with nearest-neighbor sampling. When every field is at its default, the pixels match a call that omits them. Without the capability, setting any of those fields returns `nil, "not_supported"` and draws nothing.
entries.example:
g:size()                                  -- width, height
g:clear(color)                            -- color defaults to 0
g:line(x0, y0, x1, y1, opts)
g:rect(x, y, w, h, opts)
g:circle(cx, cy, r, opts)
g:arc(cx, cy, r, start_deg, end_deg, opts)
g:polyline(points, opts)
g:polygon(points, opts)
g:pattern(x, y, w, h, opts)               -- optional capability pattern
g:text(x, y, text, opts)                  -- section 7
g:text_box(x, y, w, h, text, opts)        -- section 7
g:image(image, x, y, opts)

# 7. Text and fonts

```lua
g:text(x, y, text, opts)
g:text_box(x, y, w, h, text, opts)

local font = ctx.fonts.medium                  -- small / medium / large
local names, err = ctx.fonts:installed()       -- optional capability ttf
local font, err = ctx.fonts:open(name, px)     -- optional capability ttf
local font = ctx.fonts:size(px, sample)        -- 2.3: the preferred font at px; sample may be omitted

font.name
font.line_height
font.ascent
local width = font:measure(text)
local lines, height, consumed = font:layout(text, w, h, opts)
```

## Text options

`text` must be a valid UTF-8 string, or the call returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. Length limits: `g:text`, `g:text_box`, and `font:measure` take 8192 bytes each call, and all text in one frame totals 65536 bytes. `font:layout` takes 65536 bytes each call. Past that, the call returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`. 8192 bytes is enough to fill a whole screen on any device.

| Field | Values | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `font` | a font object | `ctx.fonts.medium` |
| `color` | 0..15 | 15 |
| `align` | `left` `center` `right`; 2.1 also has `justify` | `left` |
| `valign` | `top` `middle` `baseline` `bottom` | `top` |
| `wrap` | `word` `char` `none` | `word`, only for `text_box` and `layout` |
| `overflow` | `clip` `ellipsis` `visible` | `clip`, only for `text_box` and `layout` |
| `line_gap` | 0–255 | 0, only for `text_box` and `layout` |

## Characters

- Code points are laid out left to right. There is no bidirectional reordering and no ligation. A string that contains a right-to-left character (Arabic, Hebrew, and the like) returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`.
- A character the system fonts do not have is drawn as a missing-glyph box, and the width is the width of that box.
- A character a TTF does not have (2.5) is drawn with a system font size that has it: first the one whose line height is closest to the TTF, otherwise the next larger, then smaller ones. Its width is that size's width, and it shares the baseline with its neighbours. Only when no system font has it either is it drawn as the TTF's missing-glyph box, with the width of that box. On a host that implements 2.5, 2.0–2.4 packages draw this way too, and `measure`, `text_box`, and `layout` widths match what is drawn.
- `\t` is one space. `\n` is not drawn by `g:text` or `measure`, and its width is 0. In `text_box` and `layout` it is a forced line break. Other control characters are not drawn, and their width is 0.

## Line box and alignment

One line of text occupies one line box. The width is `font:measure(text)`. The height is `font.line_height`. The baseline is `font.ascent` pixels below the top of the line box. Alignment looks at the line box, not at the ink, so different strings in the same font share a baseline when they share an anchor.

The baseline of a system font is placed so the ink of capital Latin letters, digits, and CJK characters sits vertically centered in the line box (within 1 pixel). That is why `valign = "middle"`, vertical centering in `text_box`, and the label inside a button look centered. The descenders of lowercase letters (g, y, p) fall below the midline. On `x4_pro` and `x4_classic`, `ascent` of `small`, `medium`, and `large` is 17, 21, and 26.

`(x, y)` of `g:text` is the anchor. `align` puts `x` at the left end, the midpoint, or the right end of the line box. `valign` puts `y` at the top, the vertical midpoint, the baseline, or the bottom of the line box. When centered, the left end of the line box is `x - width // 2`. When vertically centered, the top of the line box is `y - line_height // 2`.

## Text box

`g:text_box` lays text out inside a rectangle:

- `word` breaks at whitespace, beside CJK and Thai characters, and after a Tibetan separator (such as `་`), and does not split a Latin word. A word wider than the rectangle breaks at a code point. `char` breaks only at code points. Neither separates a combining mark (such as U+0301, or a Thai or Tibetan mark above or below) from the character before it, a Thai leading vowel (เ แ โ ใ ไ) from the character after it, or a Thai following vowel (ะ า ำ ๆ) from the character before it. `none` breaks only at `\n`. Whitespace at the start and end of a line takes no width.
- Each line is aligned horizontally to the rectangle width. The block of lines is aligned vertically to the rectangle height (`baseline` is treated as `top`).
- `justify` (2.1) justifies both ends: except for the last line of each paragraph (what follows is `\n` or the end of the text) and a line that has an ellipsis, the width left in the line is shared evenly between words (at the spaces). When there are no spaces, it is shared between CJK characters. A line with a single word is treated as `left`. `g:text` treats `justify` as `left`. `layout` is not affected. The block height is `n * line_height + (n - 1) * line_gap`.
- `clip` draws only whole lines that fit. `ellipsis`, when the text does not fit, draws `…` at the end of the last line that fits (or `...` if the font has no `…`), dropping characters from the end of that line if needed. `visible` draws every line, with no height limit.
- A line that cannot wrap (`wrap` is `none`, or one word is wider than the rectangle) and runs past the width: `clip` cuts off the overflow, `ellipsis` shortens it and ends with `…`, `visible` draws it anyway.
- When not even one line fits, nothing is drawn, and the call still succeeds.

## Measurement and paging

`font:measure(text)` returns the width of a single line. `font:layout(text, w, h, opts)` lays the text out by the rules of `text_box` but does not draw. It returns three integers: the number of lines drawn, the block height of those lines, and how many bytes fit. When the bytes that fit are less than `#text`, `text:sub(consumed + 1)` is the start of the next page: a newline at the end of the page, and a space where a line wrapped, count as part of this page, so the next page does not skip them again. `consumed` is always on a code-point boundary. When the text is longer than the per-call byte limit, use the standard-library `utf8.offset` to find a code-point boundary and split there. `layout` reads only `wrap`, `overflow`, and `line_gap`.

Neither call draws anything. Both may be called from any callback, and they do not count toward the command limit.

## Fonts

`ctx.fonts.small`, `medium`, and `large` are the system fonts. Line heights are in section 3. A size whose face has no CJK (for example `small` on `x4_pro`) switches drawing and measurement to `medium` when the string contains a CJK code point.

`font.name` is the system-font size name (`"small"` and so on) or the TTF name (the one from `installed`). A TTF font also has `font.px`, the size it was opened at.

When the face switches to `medium`, the whole string is laid out as `medium`: line height, baseline, and the height `layout` returns are those of `medium`. `font.line_height` and `font.ascent` stay the values of this size.

When `ctx.capabilities.ttf` is true, `installed` and `open` exist. Otherwise they are nil. On a host that supports TTF, it is true only when this session has set aside TTF memory (the manifest has `ttf_reserve_kb`, or `requires` contains `ttf`; see Manifest in the general rules). With `ttf_reserve_kb` alone and no `requires`, the app still opens on devices without TTF and falls back to the system fonts.

TTF files are put by the user on the device storage card; an app package cannot carry TTF. The host looks in the same folders the reader picks body fonts from, in this order: `fonts/`, `font/`, the Simplified and the Traditional Chinese folders named "fonts", `Pushed Fonts/` (fonts pushed from the cloud), and the Chinese-named folder for bundled external fonts. Any font the reader can choose, apps can choose too. In each folder only files with the `.ttf` extension directly in it count; when two folders hold the same file name, the earlier folder wins. Tell users to put fonts in `fonts/`. The folders may hold none, or may not exist at all; then `installed()` returns an empty table.

- `installed()` returns the TTF names available on the device, sorted by name, with no path and no `.ttf`, each name once. When one of the folders exists but cannot be read, or the storage card is unavailable, it returns `nil, "io_error"`.
- `open(name, px)`: `name` comes from `installed`. `px` is an integer from 8 to 96, the type size. Line height is decided by the font and is `font.line_height` (usually a little larger than `px`). The same pair returns the same object. The 33rd distinct pair returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`. A missing file is `nil, "not_found"`. A face that does not fit in `ttf_reserve_kb` is `nil, "out_of_memory"`. A failed read is `nil, "io_error"`.

(2.3) `ctx.fonts:size(px, sample)` asks for type of size `px` without choosing a font:

```lua
local big = ctx.fonts:size(40)
g:text(240, 100, "12:30", { font = big, align = "center" })
```

- `px` is an integer from 8 to 96; otherwise it returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. In every other case it returns a font object. Every host that implements 2.3 has this function; it is not an optional capability.
- `sample` (2.3.1) may be omitted. It is the text this font has to draw: the chosen file must have a glyph for every character in it; spaces and control characters do not count, and an empty string accepts any file. It is at most 256 bytes. When it is not valid UTF-8, contains NUL, or contains right-to-left text (as for `g:text`), the call returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. A value that is neither a string nor nil is a Lua error.
- Without `sample` the host takes a check character from the system language (`ctx.i18n.locale`):

  | `locale` | Check character |
  |---|---|
  | `zh` | U+56FD (CJK "country") |
  | `zh-TW` | U+570B (traditional form) |
  | `ja` | U+3042 (hiragana a) and U+56FD |
  | `ko` | 한 |
  | `ru` | Ж |
  | `el` | Ω |
  | `th` | ก |
  | `bo` | ཀ |
  | `vi` | ệ |
  | `tr` | ğ |
  | `de` | ä |
  | `fr` | é |
  | `es` | ñ |
  | `it` | à |
  | `pt` | ã |
  | `pl` | ł |
  | `cs` | ř |
  | `hu` | ő |
  | `sv` | å |
  | others (`en`, `nl`, `ms`, `id`, `ar`) | A |

  So a user with an English interface and only Latin fonts still gets large type. `ar` takes A because 2.x does not draw right-to-left text.
- When this session has TTF memory (`ctx.capabilities.ttf` is true), it uses the preferred font: it tries the reader's body font, `MiSans-Regular`, `MiSans-Medium`, `MiSans-Demibold`, `MiSans` (each of these names looked up in the folder order above), then the other TTF files (in folder order, sorted by name within a folder), and takes the first one that opens and can draw the check characters. At most 8 files are tried, counting the ones listed first; when the folders hold many TTF files, later ones may not be tried. To use a particular font, `open` it by name. Once chosen for a `sample` (or for the check character when there is none), the whole session uses that file: the result is the same object as `open(its name, px)`, `font.name` is its name, `font.px` equals `px`, and it counts toward the 32 pairs.
- Pass `sample` when the text is not in the system language: a clock face that shows only digits writes `ctx.fonts:size(96, "0123456789:")` and gets large type in any interface language; a Chinese book title shown in an English interface writes `ctx.fonts:size(24, "\u{4E2D}")` (U+4E2D, a common Chinese character).
- With no TTF memory, no TTF on the card that can draw the check characters, or when this size cannot be opened (32 pairs already open, not enough memory, a failed read), it returns the system font whose line height is closest to `px` (in the order `small`, `medium`, `large`, the first closest one wins). Then `font.px` is nil and the type may be smaller than `px`.
- Calling it again with the same `px` and `sample` in the same session returns the same object.
- Lay out with the returned font's `line_height`, `measure`, and `layout`, not by reckoning from `px`. To also run on 2.2 and earlier devices, write `"api": "2.2"` or lower and first test whether `ctx.fonts.size` exists.

Every font object is used the same way, passed as `opts.font`.

`ctx.fonts:size(px)` is enough for most apps: ask for the size you need. `small`, `medium`, and `large` are only system presets and the fallback when there is no TTF; 24 for body text and 30 for titles are only common values. Games and visually rich apps should use different font sizes to suit the picture.

To let the user change fonts, list `installed()` for the user to choose from, save the chosen name in `ctx.state` (section 28), and `open` it each time; when the font was deleted or does not open, fall back to `size`. When the card holds no fonts at all, tell the user on screen to put `.ttf` files in the `fonts/` folder on the storage card.

```lua
-- the manifest has "ttf_reserve_kb": 2048
local function fonts_on_card(ctx)
  if not ctx.capabilities.ttf then return {} end
  return ctx.fonts:installed() or {}       -- treat io_error as none
end

local function body_font(ctx, px)
  local name = ctx.state.font               -- the name the user chose last time, nil if never
  local f = name and ctx.capabilities.ttf and ctx.fonts:open(name, px)
  return f or ctx.fonts:size(px)
end

-- the user picked item i in the list
local list = fonts_on_card(ctx)
ctx.state.font = list[i]
```

# 8. Packaged resources

```lua
local image, err = ctx.package:image(key)
image.width, image.height
image:release()
ctx.package:cache_stats()
ctx.package:exists(name)
ctx.package:size(name)
ctx.package:read(name)
local reader, err = ctx.package:open_text(name, opts)
```

`key` and `name` are file names. They must not contain `/` or `..`, or the call returns `nil, "invalid_argument"` (`exists` returns false).

**Images.** A packaged image is XIC, converted by the packager from PNG and the like: black and white, 4 levels, or 16 levels, with or without transparency (the packager keeps the source image's alpha channel). `image` returns an object. The same `key` returns the same object. A key not in the package is `nil, "not_found"`. A decode failure is `nil, "io_error"`. Not enough memory is `nil, "out_of_memory"`. The host keeps at most 320 decoded images at once, 524288 bytes in total. Past that it drops the one that has gone longest without being drawn (images drawn this frame or the previous frame are not dropped, so everything drawn in one frame is shown, even if the total exceeds 524288 bytes). A dropped object is decoded again the next time it is drawn, and that is invisible to the script. If decoding runs out of memory, the host drops images that are not on screen and tries once more. If that is still not enough, it returns `out_of_memory`. `release` drops the image on purpose, returns true, and may be called again. The object can still be asked for its width and height, and it can still be drawn.

`cache_stats()` returns `{ count, limit, bytes }`: how many images are cached, the limit 320, and the total bytes.

**Runtime images** (2.1): `ctx.image:decode`, `ctx.qr:encode`, and `ctx.reader:cover` also return image objects. They are used the same way, but they are not in the cache above. A session holds at most 8 of them at once, 524288 bytes in total. Asking for another returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`. The host does not drop them. `release` frees the memory. After that, `g:image` of that object returns `nil, "invalid_handle"` (width and height can still be read). They are all released when the session ends.

**Data files.** `exists`, `size`, and `read` look only at `data_files`. A name not on that list makes `size` and `read` return `nil, "not_found"`. `read` returns the whole file as a byte string. A failed read is `nil, "io_error"`. Not enough memory is `nil, "out_of_memory"`. Read a large file line by line with `open_text`.

**Line by line.** `open_text` accepts only a listed file whose name ends in `.txt` or `.tsv`. `opts.max_line_bytes` defaults to 512 and is at most 65536.

| Method | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `reader:read_line()` | The next line, with a trailing `\n` and `\r` removed. nil at the end of the file. A line that is too long returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"` and skips to the next line |
| `reader:seek(pos)` | Moves to byte `pos` and returns true. A `pos` outside `0..file length` returns `nil, "invalid_argument"` |
| `reader:tell()` | The current byte position |
| `reader:close()` | Returns nothing, and may be called again. After that the first three methods return `nil, "invalid_handle"` |

## Messages

```lua
ctx.i18n.locale
ctx.i18n:t(key, params)
```

`locale` is the system UI language. It does not change during the session:

`zh` `zh-TW` `en` `ja` `ko` `tr` `de` `fr` `es` `it` `pt` `nl` `ru` `pl` `cs` `hu` `vi` `ms` `id` `th` `el` `bo` `sv` `ar`

Message files are `lang/<locale>.tsv` inside the package. They are not listed in `data_files`. Each line is `key<TAB>value`. A BOM, an empty line, a line with no TAB, and a line that starts with `#` are ignored. The two characters `\n` in a value mean a newline.

`t` looks up `lang/<locale>.tsv`, then (for `zh-TW`) `lang/zh.tsv`, then `lang/en.tsv`. If none of them has the key, it uses `key` itself. `params` may be omitted. When it is present, `{name}` in the value is replaced with `tostring(params.name)`. A name that is not in the table is left as written. A `key` that is not a string raises a Lua error. `t` does not return an error code.

```lua
ctx.i18n:t("greeting", { name = "Ada" })   -- greeting	Hello, {name}
```

local image, err = ctx.package:image(key)
image.width, image.height
image:release()
ctx.package:cache_stats()
ctx.package:exists(name)
ctx.package:size(name)
ctx.package:read(name)
local reader, err = ctx.package:open_text(name, opts)

# 9. Private files

This is persistence the app manages itself. (2.2) Small, structured state can be left to the host's automatic save; see section 28. No permission is required. Each app has its own directory, and other apps cannot see it. The main program and the lock screen share it. Uninstall deletes it. (2.9) Files the user should see, put in, or take away use the app files in section 29.

```lua
ctx.storage:read(name)
ctx.storage:write(name, data)
ctx.storage:remove(name)
ctx.storage:exists(name)
ctx.storage:size(name)
ctx.storage:list()
ctx.storage:usage()
```

A name is 1–64 bytes, character set `[a-z0-9._-]`, and does not start or end with `.`. An illegal name returns `nil, "invalid_argument"` (`exists` returns false). `data` is a string and may contain any bytes.

Quota: one file is at most 262144 bytes, there are at most 512 files, and the total is at most 134217728 bytes (128 MB, exactly 512 full files). A `write` that would exceed any of those returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`, and the previous file is unchanged. A failed read or write, a missing card, or a card without enough free space returns `nil, "io_error"`. The quota is a ceiling, not a reservation: when the card is nearly full, a write can fail before the quota is reached.

| Call | File exists | File is absent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `read` | the byte string | `nil, "not_found"` |
| `write` | replaces the whole file, returns true | creates it, returns true |
| `remove` | deletes it, returns true | returns true |
| `exists` | true | false |
| `size` | the byte count | `nil, "not_found"` |

`list()` returns an array sorted by the byte order of the names. `usage()` returns `{ files, bytes, max_files, max_bytes }`.

If power fails during `write`, a later read sees either the whole old content or the whole new content.

Reading and writing the storage card is slow, and the time counts against the limit of the current callback. Reference values measured on Gancao firmware (4 KB file, not guarantees): on the X4 Pro a write takes about 120 ms, a read about 35 ms, a remove about 70 ms; on the X4 Classic about 30 ms, 8 ms and 13 ms. On the X4 Pro, writing ten files in one callback already exceeds the 1000 ms limit. Combine the data you save into one file; if you really need to write many files, spread them over several `ctx:after` callbacks, a few at a time. Do not write files on every frame in `on_tick` or `on_draw`.

Store tables as JSON from section 10.
entries.example:
ctx.storage:read(name)
ctx.storage:write(name, data)
ctx.storage:remove(name)
ctx.storage:exists(name)
ctx.storage:size(name)
ctx.storage:list()
ctx.storage:usage()

# 10. JSON

```lua
local s, err = ctx.json:encode(value)
local value, err = ctx.json:decode(s)
ctx.json.null
```

**encode** accepts booleans, numbers, strings, and tables, and does not accept nil. Table rules:

- Keys that are exactly the contiguous integers `1..n` (or an empty table) encode as an array. Keys that are all strings encode as an object. A mix returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`.
- `ctx.json.null` encodes as `null`.
- A function, coroutine, object, cyclic reference, nesting deeper than 32, NaN, or infinity returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`.
- Object keys are written in byte order. A float uses the shortest decimal that restores that single-precision value. The result is at most 262144 bytes; otherwise `nil, "limit_exceeded"`.

**decode** returns the matching Lua value: an array becomes a table with keys `1..n`, an object becomes a table with string keys, and `null` becomes `ctx.json.null`. An integer that fits in 32 bits is an integer; otherwise it is a float. Input that is not valid JSON, or nesting deeper than 32, returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`.

Encoding and decoding time counts against the limit of the current callback. Reference values measured on Gancao firmware (not guarantees): about 1.6 µs per byte (X4 Pro) and 2.2 µs (X4 Classic); encoding and then decoding 200 small records (four fields each) takes about 35 ms and 47 ms. Encode or decode large data once when you need it, not on every frame.
entries.example:
local s, err = ctx.json:encode(value)
local value, err = ctx.json:decode(s)
ctx.json.null

entries.content:
# 11. Offscreen layers

```lua
local layer, err = ctx.layers:create(w, h)
layer.width, layer.height
layer:draw(function(g) end)
g:image(layer, x, y, opts)
layer:release()
```

`w` and `h` are integers from 1 to `max(ctx.screen.width, ctx.screen.height)`. The buffer is `w * h` pixels. Each pixel is a `gray_levels` color plus 1 bit of transparency. A new layer is fully transparent. At most 4 exist at once. The 5th returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`. Not enough memory returns `nil, "out_of_memory"`.

`draw` calls the function immediately and passes the layer's canvas. The origin is the layer's top left. Every drawing call from sections 6 and 7 is available. They draw straight into the buffer and do not count toward the per-frame command limit. `draw` may be called from any callback, to prepare content ahead of time. It cannot nest (calling it from another `draw` or from `on_draw` returns `nil, "busy"`). An error inside the function propagates as it is, and the buffer keeps the pixels from before the call. Success returns nothing.

`release` returns true and may be called again. After that, `draw` and a `g:image` that uses the layer as its source return `nil, "invalid_handle"`.

Blit it back to the screen, or onto another layer, with `g:image`. A layer carries its own transparency: a new layer is fully transparent, a pixel that has been drawn becomes opaque, and `g:clear(color)` makes the whole layer that opaque color.
entries.example:
local layer, err = ctx.layers:create(w, h)
layer.width, layer.height
layer:draw(function(g) end)
g:image(layer, x, y, opts)
layer:release()

entries.content:
# 12. Clock, log, and memory

```lua
ctx.clock:millis()
local t = ctx.clock:now()
ctx.log:info(msg)  ctx.log:warn(msg)  ctx.log:error(msg)
ctx.gc:collect()
ctx.gc:count()
```

`millis` returns milliseconds since this boot, in `0..2147483647`. After about 24.8 days it returns to 0. The gap between two samples is `(later - earlier) & 0x7FFFFFFF`, which stays correct across the wrap.

`now` returns a read-only table. Several calls in the same callback see the same snapshot.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `valid` | Whether the time may be shown to the user |
| `year` `month` `day` | Gregorian date. Month 1–12, day 1–31 |
| `hour` `minute` `second` | 0–23, 0–59, 0–59 |
| `weekday` | 0 is Sunday |
| `hour12` | Whether the system displays a 12-hour clock. It does not change `hour` |
| `date_order` | 2.5: the system date order, `"ymd"`, `"mdy"`, or `"dmy"` |
| `date_sep` | 2.5: the system date separator, `"/"` or `"-"` |
| `offset_minutes` | Minutes from UTC, including daylight saving |
| `epoch_sec` | UTC Unix seconds. nil when it does not fit in a 32-bit integer (after 2038-01-19) |
| `local_sec` | `epoch_sec + offset_minutes * 60`. nil when it is out of range |
| `revision` | Increments when the time is set again, or the time zone, the 12/24-hour mode, or the date format (2.5) changes. 1 at the start of the session |

When `valid` is false, the date, the clock time, `weekday`, `epoch_sec`, and `local_sec` are nil. `valid`, `hour12`, `offset_minutes`, and `revision` always have a value, and from 2.5 so do `date_order` and `date_sep`.

Order a displayed date by the user's setting, not by guessing from `locale`:

```lua
local t = ctx.clock:now()
local parts = { y = t.year, m = string.format("%02d", t.month), d = string.format("%02d", t.day) }
local o = t.date_order or "ymd"   -- hosts before 2.5 do not have this field
local s = parts[o:sub(1, 1)] .. (t.date_sep or "/") .. parts[o:sub(2, 2)] .. (t.date_sep or "/") .. parts[o:sub(3, 3)]
```

There is no event for a time change. A clock face compares `revision` each time it wakes, and realigns when it changed. To land on the next minute: `ctx:after((60 - t.second) * 1000, fn)`, then read `now()` again on waking, because the wake can be a few hundred milliseconds late.

The three `log` methods take one string and return nothing. A non-string raises a Lua error. A log line may be dropped when space runs out. That is not an error.

`collect` runs one full collection. `count` returns how many bytes the script heap currently occupies.
entries.example:
ctx.clock:millis()
local t = ctx.clock:now()
ctx.log:info(msg)  ctx.log:warn(msg)  ctx.log:error(msg)
ctx.gc:collect()
ctx.gc:count()

# 13. Device status

```lua
local b = ctx.device:battery()   -- { percent, charging }
local r = ctx.device:radios()    -- { wifi_on, wifi_connected, bluetooth_on }
```

No permission is required. `percent` is an integer 0–100, or -1 when it cannot be read. `charging` is a boolean, or false when it cannot be read. The three fields of `radios` are booleans.

2.1 also has: `voltage_mv` (battery voltage in millivolts) and `temperature_c` (battery temperature in degrees Celsius, an integer) on `battery()`, nil when they cannot be read. When the `net` permission is declared, `radios()` also has `wifi_ssid` (the network name) and `wifi_signal` (signal, 0–4 bars) while Wi-Fi is connected, and nil when it is not.

local b = ctx.device:battery()   -- { percent, charging }
local r = ctx.device:radios()    -- { wifi_on, wifi_connected, bluetooth_on }

# 14. Networking

Requires the `net` permission. When it is not declared, `ctx.net` is nil. It is also nil in a lock-screen session.

```lua
local job, err = ctx.net:request({
  url = "https://example.com/api",
  method = "POST",                 -- "GET" (the default) or "POST"
  headers = { ["content-type"] = "application/json" },
  body = ctx.json:encode({ q = 1 }),
}, function(ctx, res)
  if res.ok and res.status == 200 then
    data = ctx.json:decode(res.body)
    ctx:invalidate()
  end
end)
job:cancel()
```

**Request.**

- `url` starts with `http://` or `https://` and is at most 1024 bytes. https is checked with the device's built-in root certificates, so https fails when the clock is not valid (`io_error`).
- `body` is used only for `POST`. It is a string, at most 65536 bytes, default the empty string. A `GET` that sets `body` returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`.
- `headers` is a table of string to string, at most 16 items. A name is ≤ 64 bytes and a value is ≤ 1024 bytes. A `POST` that does not set `content-type` uses `text/plain; charset=utf-8`.
- Redirects are not followed. A 3xx is handed to the app as it is. `res.headers.location` is the target.
- When Wi-Fi is off but a network has been saved, the host turns it on and connects. The whole request has at most 30000 ms from the call: if Wi-Fi is not connected in that time, the result is `no_network`; if it connected and the response is still not complete, the result is `timeout`. How long Wi-Fi that was turned on for a request stays on afterwards is described under “Keeping Wi-Fi on” below.

Only one request may be unfinished at a time. Another `request` returns `nil, "busy"`. After `job:cancel()`, the cancelled request keeps its place until the host has finished aborting it, usually a second or two and at most until its 30000 ms deadline; during that time `request` also returns `nil, "busy"`, so try again a little later (for example with `ctx:after`). An illegal argument returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. Success returns the request object.

When `ok` is true, `status`, `headers`, `body`, and `bytes` all have values. When https fails and `ctx.clock:now().valid` is false, the clock is usually not set. Tell the user to go online and set the time first.

The **completion function** is called once as a callback after the request ends. The arguments are `ctx` and the result table:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `ok` | true when a complete HTTP response was received (any status code) |
| `status` | The status code. nil when no response was received |
| `headers` | Response headers, names lowercased. The same name is joined with `, `. At most 32 items, 4096 bytes in total |
| `body` | The response body, at most 131072 bytes kept |
| `bytes` | The total body size in bytes, including the part that was cut off |
| `err` | See the table below |

| `err` | When |
| --- | --- |
| nil | Success |
| `no_network` | No saved Wi-Fi, or it did not connect within 30000 ms |
| `timeout` | After connecting, 30000 ms from the call passed before the response was complete |
| `io_error` | The connection dropped, DNS or TLS failed, or the host cannot start a request right now |
| `limit_exceeded` | The body was longer than 131072 bytes and was cut off. `ok` is still true |

`job:cancel()` cancels an unfinished request. The completion function is not called. It returns nothing. It has no effect on a request that has already ended. An unfinished request is cancelled automatically when the session ends.

## Keeping Wi-Fi on (2.4)

```lua
ctx.net:keep_wifi(ms)
```

When the user has Wi-Fi turned off in the system, the host turns it on for a request (see “Request” above). Turning it on, connecting, and getting an address usually take several seconds, so the host does not turn it off as soon as the request ends; it keeps it on for a while:

- This applies only to Wi-Fi the host turned on for a request. If the user has Wi-Fi on, it stays on regardless of this setting.
- After the last request ends (completes or `job:cancel()`), Wi-Fi stays on for `ms` milliseconds. A request made during that time uses the existing connection, and the timer restarts when it ends. If no new request comes before the time runs out, the host turns Wi-Fi off.
- `ms` is an integer from -1 to 2147483647 (`math.maxinteger`, about 24.8 days); the default is 300000 (5 minutes). 0 turns Wi-Fi off as soon as a request ends; -1 keeps it on until the session ends, for the whole time the app is open. Every session starts with the default.
- Keeping starts only with the first request: calling `keep_wifi` does not turn Wi-Fi on. To be connected as soon as the app opens, make the first request in `on_load`.
- A new value takes effect at once and still counts from the end of the last request: if a smaller value has already passed, Wi-Fi is turned off within about 1 second. Changing to -1 while it is being kept means it is no longer turned off.
- When the session ends (the app exits, the lock screen starts, or the device powers off), Wi-Fi is turned off at once without waiting for the remaining time.
- Success returns nothing. If `ms` is a number but not an integer in this range (such as -2 or 1.5), it returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. If it is not a number (a string, or missing), it raises a Lua error.

A host that implements 2.4 keeps Wi-Fi on for 5 minutes by default for every 2.x package. A host of 2.3 or earlier has no such function: it turns Wi-Fi off as soon as a request ends, and the next request connects again. A package that declares `"2.3"` or lower should first check that `ctx.net.keep_wifi` exists.

### Choosing how long to keep it

The longer Wi-Fi stays on, the faster consecutive requests are, and the more power it uses (with Wi-Fi on, the whole device draws several times as much power as with it off, and battery life shrinks accordingly). Choose by how the app uses the network:

| How the app uses the network | What to write | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fetches data once when it opens and never again (a daily poem, a quick look at the weather) | `keep_wifi(0)` | Off as soon as it is done; uses the least power |
| Requests only when the user acts (load on page turn, search, tap to refresh) | Nothing; the default is 5 minutes | Consecutive actions do not wait to reconnect |
| Polls at an interval under 5 minutes (LAN sensors, server status, every 10–60 seconds) | Nothing; to save power, about “interval × 2”, for example `keep_wifi(90000)` for every 40 seconds | The keep time must be longer than the interval plus the request itself, or every round reconnects |
| Polls every 5 to 30 minutes | `keep_wifi(interval + 60000)` | The 5-minute default is too short, and every round would reconnect for several seconds |
| Polls at intervals over 30 minutes | Your choice: if power matters, write nothing or `keep_wifi(0)`; if every request should be fast, `keep_wifi(interval + 60000)` or `-1` | With long intervals a few seconds of reconnecting each round is usually acceptable, and staying on uses more power |
| Must stay online the whole time the app is open (live dashboards, remote controls, LAN chat, continuous reporting) | `keep_wifi(-1)`, and make the first request in `on_load` | The network stays up while the app is open and goes off only on exit or lock screen |

The interval is the time from the end of one request to the start of the next. If the keep time is shorter, every round waits for Wi-Fi to reconnect, and the user sees requests that are “slow and laggy”.

Example: check a server on the LAN every 40 seconds.

```lua
local POLL_MS = 40000
local status

local function poll(ctx)
  local job = ctx.net:request({ url = "http://192.168.1.20:8080/status" }, function(ctx, res)
    if res.ok and res.status == 200 then
      status = ctx.json:decode(res.body)
      ctx:invalidate()
    end
    ctx:after(POLL_MS, poll)        -- wait 40 seconds after the previous one ends
  end)
  if not job then
    ctx:after(1000, poll)           -- busy and the like: try again shortly
  end
end

function on_load(ctx)
  if ctx.net.keep_wifi then         -- not on hosts of 2.3 or earlier
    ctx.net:keep_wifi(POLL_MS * 2 + 10000)
  end
  poll(ctx)
end
```

- Schedule the next round with `ctx:after` in the completion function, not with a fixed-period timer: slow requests then do not pile up (only one request may run at a time).
- `keep_wifi(-1)` suits apps the user watches, or that are always plugged in. Ordinary apps should use a specific number of milliseconds, so Wi-Fi turns itself off when the user leaves the device alone.
- Poll only while the app is in the foreground. Entering the lock screen or exiting the app ends the session and turns Wi-Fi off; the next open starts over.

## Connection reuse (2.6)

A host that implements 2.6 keeps the connection after a request ends. The next request to the same origin (same scheme, host, and port) uses that connection instead of setting up TCP and TLS again. On a LAN, back-to-back requests usually drop from a few hundred milliseconds to a few tens; https saves more. This is host behaviour: the interface and results do not change, and 2.0–2.5 packages benefit too.

- When the server closes a kept connection, or it goes stale after idling too long, the host reconnects by itself and resends a request that was not sent. A `POST` is resent only when it had not gone out yet, so the server never receives it twice.
- When the app sets `connection: close` itself, the connection closes when that request ends.
- All kept connections close when the session ends or Wi-Fi turns off.

## WebSocket (2.6)

```lua
local ws, err = ctx.net:websocket({
  url = "wss://game.example.com/room/42",
  headers = { authorization = "Bearer ..." },
}, {
  on_open = function(ctx, ws)
    ws:send(ctx.json:encode({ type = "join" }))
  end,
  on_message = function(ctx, ws, data, binary)
    local msg = ctx.json:decode(data)
    ctx:invalidate()
  end,
  on_close = function(ctx, ws, code, reason, err)
    -- the connection ended; err is nil for a normal close
  end,
})
ws:send("hello")
ws:close()
```

A persistent two-way connection: once it is up, the server can send messages at any time and the app can send messages at any time, without a new request each time. It suits matches, chat, live dashboards, and other apps that must know at once when the other side does something. For fetching data now and then, use `request` above.

**Connecting.**

- `url` starts with `ws://` or `wss://` and is at most 1024 bytes. `wss` is checked against the device's built-in root certificates, like https, and fails when the clock is invalid.
- `headers` follows the same rules as `request` (at most 16 entries, names ≤ 64 bytes, values ≤ 1024 bytes). The host fills in `host`, `upgrade`, `connection`, and names starting with `sec-websocket-`; if the app sets one, the call returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`.
- `protocol` is optional: a subprotocol name string of 1–64 bytes, containing only letters, digits, and `-_.`. The handshake fails when the server does not accept it.
- The second argument is the callback table: `on_message` is required, `on_open` and `on_close` are optional. Any other type raises a Lua error.
- Only one connection at a time. While a connection has not ended (including while it is closing), another `websocket` returns `nil, "busy"`; a new connection can be opened right away inside `on_close`. Invalid arguments return `nil, "invalid_argument"`. On success it returns the connection object, which is not connected yet.
- Wi-Fi is turned on automatically, as for `request`. If the handshake does not complete within 30000 ms of the call, the connection ends: `no_network` when Wi-Fi never connected, `timeout` when it timed out after Wi-Fi connected, and `io_error` for DNS or TLS failures or when the server refuses the upgrade (answers with something other than 101).

**Callbacks** are callbacks in the sense of section 2, with a 1000 ms limit:

| Callback | When |
| --- | --- |
| `on_open(ctx, ws)` | The handshake completed and messages can be sent. At most once per connection |
| `on_message(ctx, ws, data, binary)` | A complete message arrived. `data` is a string; `binary` is true for a binary frame and false for a text frame (the host does not check that text is valid UTF-8). Fragmented messages are joined before they reach the app |
| `on_close(ctx, ws, code, reason, err)` | The connection ended. Exactly once per connection; no callbacks for this connection come after it |

`on_close` parameters:

| Parameter | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `code` | Close code, an integer. When the other side or the app sent a close frame, that frame's code (1005 when the frame has none); 1006 when the connection did not close normally (network lost, timeout, handshake failed) |
| `reason` | Close reason string, possibly empty |
| `err` | nil when both sides closed normally; otherwise see the table below |

| `err` | When |
| --- | --- |
| `no_network` | No saved Wi-Fi, or Wi-Fi did not connect within 30000 ms |
| `timeout` | The handshake ran past its deadline, or nothing arrived from the other side for 45000 ms while connected |
| `io_error` | DNS or TLS failure, the server refused the upgrade, the connection dropped, Wi-Fi dropped |
| `limit_exceeded` | The other side sent a message over 131072 bytes; the host closes with 1009 |

**Sending.**

```lua
local ok, err = ws:send(data, binary)
```

- `data` is a string of at most 65536 bytes. With `binary` true it goes as a binary frame; omitted or false, as a text frame.
- The send is queued and true is returned at once, without waiting for the other side to receive it. The host sends in call order.
- Before `on_open` it returns `nil, "inactive"`; after the connection ended or `ws:close` was called, `nil, "invalid_handle"`; over 65536 bytes, `nil, "limit_exceeded"`; when more than 16 sends, or more than 131072 bytes in total, are queued and not yet sent, `nil, "busy"`.

**Closing.**

```lua
ws:close(code, reason)
```

- `code` is optional: 1000 (the default) or 3000–4999. `reason` is optional, at most 123 bytes. Out-of-range values return `nil, "invalid_argument"`.
- The host sends a close frame and waits for the other side to answer, at most 5000 ms, then disconnects and calls `on_close` (`code` is the app's code, `err` is nil). Called before the connection is up, it simply abandons the connection; `on_close` then has `code` 1006 and `err` nil.
- Returns nothing on success; has no effect on a connection that has already ended or is closing.

**What the host handles.**

- Heartbeat: after 20000 ms of idle the host sends a ping, and it answers the other side's pings with pongs; control frames are not passed to the app. When nothing (including pongs) arrives from the other side for 45000 ms, the connection counts as lost, with `err` `timeout`. Apps do not write their own heartbeat.
- No automatic reconnect: when the connection drops, the host calls `on_close`, and the app decides whether and when to reconnect (see "How to build an online game" below).
- While paused (section 2) the connection stays up and the heartbeat goes on. Received messages, `on_open`, and `on_close` queue up in order and are called one by one after `on_resume`. When messages not yet passed to the app exceed 262144 bytes in total (usually during a pause, but slow callbacks can cause it too), the host closes the connection with 1009 and `err` `limit_exceeded`.
- When the session ends (exiting the app, entering the lock screen, powering off) the host closes the connection with 1001 and does not call `on_close`.
- Wi-Fi: Wi-Fi turned on automatically stays on while the connection is open. After the connection ends, the "keep Wi-Fi" timer runs; a WebSocket ending counts the same as a request ending. While the connection is open the host may turn off Wi-Fi power saving: lower latency, more power use; see "How to build an online game" below.
- The connection and `request` do not block each other: requests can be made while the connection is open.

## How to build an online game (2.6)

First pick the connection type for the game's pace:

| Game | Use | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Turn-based, slow-paced (chess, go, crosswords, a daily puzzle) | `request`, asking every few seconds while waiting for the opponent; or WebSocket | One request per move is enough; from 2.6, back-to-back requests reuse the connection, a few tens of milliseconds on a LAN |
| Must know at once what the other side did (card games, draw-and-guess, multiplayer quizzes, chat) | WebSocket | The server pushes messages as soon as it has them, no polling |
| Fast action (shooters, racing, fighting) | Not suitable | An e-ink refresh takes a few hundred milliseconds; players cannot see changes that fast |

The device works the same way as online games on phones and the web: HTTP(S) and WebSocket only, no raw TCP or UDP. Write the server for the standard WebSocket protocol (a server a browser can connect to, the device can connect to too).

**Design points.**

- The server decides: the device only sends what it wants to do (play a card, place a stone); the server rules on it and pushes the result to everyone. That makes disconnects, cheating, and two players acting at once easy to handle.
- Keep messages small and few: short JSON, one thing per message. Call `ctx:invalidate()` only when the state changes; drawing once after several messages is fine too (the e-ink refresh is slower than the network).
- Disconnects will happen: the user locks the screen, walks out of Wi-Fi range, the server restarts. In `on_close`, reconnect after a few seconds with `ctx:after`, doubling the interval after each failure up to 30–60 seconds. After reconnecting, have the server send the full current state again; do not assume nothing happened while disconnected.
- Give every message a sequence or turn number, and drop old ones.
- Entering the lock screen or exiting the app closes the connection; the next open reconnects and fetches the state again. To continue the last match, keep the room number in `ctx.state` (section 28).
- Power: while the connection is open Wi-Fi stays on and power saving may be off, so power use is much higher than usual. Call `ws:close()` when the match ends; in the lobby or while waiting for a match, `request` alone may be enough.

Example: connect to a match server and reconnect automatically after a disconnect.

```lua
local URL = "wss://game.example.com/room/"
local state = { seq = 0 }
local conn
local retry_ms = 2000

local function connect(ctx)
  local ws = ctx.net:websocket({ url = URL .. ctx.state.room }, {
    on_open = function(ctx, ws)
      retry_ms = 2000
      ws:send(ctx.json:encode({ type = "hello", seq = state.seq }))
    end,
    on_message = function(ctx, ws, data)
      local msg = ctx.json:decode(data)
      if msg and msg.seq > state.seq then   -- drop old messages
        state = msg
        ctx:invalidate()
      end
    end,
    on_close = function(ctx, ws, code, reason, err)
      conn = nil
      ctx:invalidate()
      if code ~= 1000 then                  -- not a normal end: reconnect after a while
        ctx:after(retry_ms, connect)
        retry_ms = math.min(retry_ms * 2, 60000)
      end
    end,
  })
  if ws then
    conn = ws
  else
    ctx:after(retry_ms, connect)            -- busy and the like: try again later
  end
end

function on_load(ctx)
  ctx.state.room = ctx.state.room or "42"
  connect(ctx)
end

local function play(ctx, move)
  if conn and conn:send(ctx.json:encode({ type = "move", move = move })) then
    return true
  end
  ctx.dialog:toast("Reconnecting")
end
```

- Call `play` from `on_input`. When sending fails (not connected yet, reconnecting), tell the user and do not change the local state; wait for the server's result.
- When the match ends the server sends an "end" message and the app calls `conn:close()` (close code 1000, no reconnect).

  headers = { ["content-type"] = "application/json" },
  body = ctx.json:encode({ q = 1 }),

# 15. Lock screen

An app can provide a lock-screen picture, refreshed on an interval while the device is locked (a clock, a calendar, a to-do list).

While locked, the device is in deep sleep and does not keep memory. Each refresh is therefore its own short session: load the lock-screen script, draw one frame, and end. The main program and the lock screen exchange data only through the files in section 9 and (2.2) `ctx.state` from section 28. A lock-screen session does not save `ctx.state` automatically; if it changes it, it must call `ctx:save_state()` itself.

## Make this the lock screen

When the manifest has `lockscreen`, `ctx.lockscreen` exists in the main program. Otherwise it is nil:

```lua
ctx.lockscreen:set_default()
ctx.lockscreen:is_default()
ctx.lockscreen:clear_default()            -- 2.8
local ok, err = ctx.lockscreen:set_wallpaper(image)   -- 2.8
ctx.lockscreen:is_wallpaper()             -- 2.8
ctx.lockscreen:clear_wallpaper()          -- 2.9
```

`set_default` returns nothing. After the current callback returns, the host shows the system confirmation. The app receives `on_pause`, then `on_resume`. Inside `on_resume`, `is_default` is already the user's choice. If it is already the lock screen, no dialog is shown. The user can switch it back in system settings at any time. The app is not notified. Call `is_default` whenever the answer is needed.

**The lock screen and the cover are two separate things (2.9).** The lock screen (`set_default`, or the user's choice in system settings) decides what the lock screen shows when the user is not reading. The cover (`set_wallpaper`) only decides the picture drawn over the book page while reading. The two are saved separately and can both exist. Setting one does not replace the other, and clearing one does not affect the other: the same app can be the lock screen (`is_default` is true) and have a cover (`is_wallpaper` is true) at once. On a 2.8 host the two share one slot, and the one set later replaces the earlier one.

**Giving the lock screen back (2.8).** `clear_default()` returns nothing and shows no dialog. When this app is the lock screen (`is_default`), the system lock screen returns to whatever the user had chosen before this app took over, and `is_default` becomes false afterwards. The cover is not affected (2.9; on a 2.8 host the cover is given back too). When it is not the lock screen, it has no effect. Use it for an in-app “stop using as lock screen” switch.

**Clearing the cover (2.9).** `clear_wallpaper()` returns nothing and shows no dialog. When this app has a cover (`is_wallpaper`), it removes it. Afterwards `is_wallpaper` is false and the lock screen no longer draws a picture over the page while reading. The lock screen is not affected. When there is no cover, it has no effect. Use it for an in-app “stop using as cover” switch.

**Lock-screen wallpaper (2.8).** `set_wallpaper(image)` scales an image (section 8, a package image or a runtime image) or an off-screen layer (section 11) to the full portrait screen and saves it as this app's lock-screen wallpaper. The host stores it at the device's gray depth. This picture is a “cover” for reading, and it is drawn only while reading (2.8.4):

- **Reading when the device locks** (the system reader is in the foreground: EPUB, TXT, XTC, and so on): the picture is drawn over the page being read. Transparent areas show the page, and opaque areas cover it. With no transparent pixels it is the whole picture. When the reader has a menu, table of contents, or popup open, what is underneath is still the book page, not the menu. In landscape reading the lock screen stays landscape: the picture is turned upright for the reading direction and centered, and the parts outside the screen are cut off.
- **Not reading when the device locks** (home, bookshelf, system settings, an Ink App, and so on): the picture is not drawn. The lock screen shows the current lock screen as usual: when this app (or another app) is the lock screen, its lock-screen session runs; otherwise it is the user's choice in system settings (default wallpaper, book cover, custom wallpaper, live desktop, and so on).
- The lock-screen previews in system settings and the phone app follow the same rules: while reading they preview the cover over the page; otherwise they preview the current lock screen.

While reading, the lock screen draws only the cover: no lock-screen session runs and there are no timed wakes. To change the picture, call it again. The device has only one cover at a time: another app setting a cover replaces this app's (`is_wallpaper` becomes false). When the user picks a lock screen again on the lock-screen page of system settings, the cover is cleared too. Changing the lock screen elsewhere (such as “Set as wallpaper” in the image viewer, or the phone app) does not necessarily clear the cover. To know whether the cover is still there, call `is_wallpaper` whenever the answer is needed.

- When this app is already the lock screen or already has a cover, it takes effect at once and returns `true`.
- Otherwise it returns `true`, and after the current callback returns the host shows the same system confirmation as `set_default`: the app receives `on_pause`, then `on_resume`, and inside `on_resume` `is_wallpaper` is already the user's choice. If the user declines, the image is discarded. Calling again before the dialog appears returns `nil, "busy"`.
- Setting a cover does not change `is_default` (2.9; on a 2.8 host `is_default` is false once it is the cover). When this app already has a cover, `set_default` makes it the lock screen at once without a dialog. After it returns, `is_default` is already true, the cover is kept, and `is_wallpaper` is still true (2.9; on a 2.8 host `is_wallpaper` becomes false).
- An `image` that is not an image or a layer returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. One already released returns `nil, "invalid_handle"`. Out of memory returns `nil, "out_of_memory"`. A read or write failure returns `nil, "io_error"`.

As with `is_default`, the app is not notified when the user changes it in system settings. Call `is_wallpaper` when the answer is needed.

## When it runs

Whether to lock, and when, is the system's decision (idle timeout or the power key). When the lock-screen app is this app:

1. If an app is in the foreground, end its session first (`on_leave`).
2. Run one lock-screen session. `ctx.lock.reason` is `"first"`.
3. Sleep until the next whole multiple of `interval_sec` (local time: an interval of 60 wakes on the minute). When the clock is not valid, sleep for `interval_sec` seconds.
4. Wake and run one lock-screen session. `reason` is `"timer"`. Go back to step 3.

A device with no timer wake does only step 2.

## One lock-screen session

`on_load(ctx)`, then `on_draw(ctx, g)`, then the host presents the frame and ends. The two callbacks together are at most 2000 ms, and that cannot be extended. Those are the only two callbacks. `ctx:after` and `ctx:set_tick` do nothing. `ctx.budget:extend()` returns `nil, "inactive"`.

The canvas starts as paper each time, and the callback draws a complete frame. The default is a full refresh for `first` and a partial refresh for `timer`. Calling `ctx:invalidate("full")` from `on_load` or `on_draw` changes it to a full refresh. The host keeps the count of consecutive partial refreshes in a record that survives sleep, and it still inserts the automatic full refresh.

`ctx` in a lock-screen session is the same as in the main program. `require` works as usual, and the screen orientation still follows `display.orientation` in the manifest. Only these differ: `ctx.lock` exists; `ctx.net` and `ctx.lockscreen` are nil; `ctx.input:text` returns `nil, "inactive"`; `ctx:after` and `ctx:set_tick` do nothing; `ctx.budget:extend()` returns `nil, "inactive"`. A device whose `ctx.device.lock_timer` is false runs only the `first` session.

In a timer wake (`reason` is `"timer"`), the host does not turn on Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, regardless of the user's switches: `wifi_on`, `wifi_connected`, and `bluetooth_on` from `ctx.device:radios()` are all false. After the user leaves the lock screen with the power key, the radios return to the user's settings. The `first` session is not affected.

```lua
ctx.lock.reason        -- "first" | "timer"
ctx.lock.elapsed_sec   -- seconds since the previous lock-screen present; 0 for first
ctx.lock.interval_sec  -- the current interval
ctx.lock:set_interval(seconds)
```

`ctx.lock` exists only in a lock-screen session. The argument of `set_interval` is an integer from 30 to 3600. It takes effect starting with the sleep after this session, and returns nothing. The next time the lock screen is entered, it starts again from the manifest value.

The session still runs when the clock is not valid. `ctx.clock:now().valid` is false, and the script decides what to draw.

## Exceptions

- If the lock-screen script errors or runs out of time, the host draws the system default lock-screen picture and stops timer wakes until the next time the lock screen is entered.
- Below 5% battery and not charging: the script does not run. The host draws the low-battery picture and powers off.
- The power key: leave the lock screen and return to the system. The app that was in the foreground before the lock screen opens again, as a brand-new session.

ctx.lockscreen:is_default()
ctx.lockscreen:clear_default()            -- 2.8
local ok, err = ctx.lockscreen:set_wallpaper(image)   -- 2.8
ctx.lockscreen:is_wallpaper()             -- 2.8
ctx.lockscreen:clear_wallpaper()          -- 2.9

# 16. UI library

Optional capability `ui`: when it is true, `ctx.ui` exists. Otherwise it is nil. Immediate mode: every frame, declare the controls again inside `on_draw`. The library draws them, hit-tests them, and keeps focus.

```lua
local ui = ctx.ui:create()        -- create it once in on_load

function on_draw(ctx, g)
  ui:begin_frame(g)
  ui:label("title", { x = 20, y = 20, w = 440, h = 40, text = "Settings", font = ctx.fonts.large })
  ui:switch("wifi", { x = 20, y = 80, w = 440, h = 56, text = "Wi-Fi", selected = wifi })
  ui:button("save", { x = 20, y = 160, w = 200, h = 56, text = "Save", radius = 8 })
  ui:end_frame()
end

function on_input(ctx, ev)
  local id, action = ui:handle_event(ev)
  if action == "activate" then
    if id == "wifi" then wifi = not wifi end
    ctx:invalidate()
    return true
  end
  if action then ctx:invalidate(); return true end
  return false
end
```

`begin_frame` returns `nil, "busy"` when the previous frame had no `end_frame`. `end_frame` returns `nil, "invalid_argument"` when there was no `begin_frame`. The library does not clear the screen. Call `g:clear()` yourself before `begin_frame`. Controls default to `ctx.fonts.medium` and color 15.

Each control's `id` is a non-empty string, and it cannot repeat in the same frame (a repeat returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`). `x`, `y`, `w`, and `h` are required. `w` and `h` are at least 1. More than 128 controls in one frame, or a container nested more than 16 deep, returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`, and that control is not drawn.

| Control | Fields | How it is drawn |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `text` `font` `color` `align` `valign` | Drawn in the box as `text_box`, with `overflow` of `ellipsis` |
| `button` | `text` `font` `radius` `image` `border` | A stroked rounded box, text centered. When focus is drawn, the fill is 15 and the text is 0. (2.8) With `border = false` no stroke is drawn; focus still fills |
| `switch` | `text` `font` `selected` | Text on the left, an `h × h` box on the right, filled when `selected`. When focus is drawn, the stroke is 2 |
| `image` | `source` | An image object scaled to `w × h` |
| `field` (2.9) | `text` `font` `radius` `placeholder` and others | A text field. See “Text fields (2.9)” |
| `row` `column` | `gap` `children` | See below |

`children` of `row` and `column` is an array. Each item is `{ kind = "button", id = "...", w = ..., h = ..., ... }`, with no `x` or `y`. A `row` lays out left to right from its own `(x, y)`, tops aligned. A `column` lays out top to bottom, left edges aligned. Neighbors are separated by `gap` (default 0). Anything past the container is clipped.

**Image buttons (2.8)**: a `button`'s `image` is an image object (section 8), scaled to `w × h` to fill the button. With `text`, the text is centered on the image (color 15). When focus is drawn there is no fill; instead a 2-pixel frame is drawn 3 pixels outside the button (with `radius`, its corners are rounded by radius + 3). An `image` that is not an image object, or a `border` that is not a boolean, returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`.

```lua
ui:button("feed", { x = 40, y = 600, w = 96, h = 96, image = ctx.package:image("bowl"), border = false })
```

**Hit testing**: the last `button`, `switch`, or (2.9) `field` added this frame that contains the point.

**Focus**: hittable controls are ordered by when they were added. Focus is kept across frames by `id` and checked at `end_frame`: if that `id` is absent this frame, focus falls on the first one. If nothing is hittable, focus is empty.

`ctx.ui:create()` can be called more than once. Each UI object keeps its own focus, independent of the others; an object whose `begin_frame` is not called keeps its focus unchanged.

`handle_event(ev)` returns `id, action`. When there is no matching action it returns nil, nil:

| Input | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `down` of `ok` | The focused control, `press` |
| `up` of `ok`, and focus did not move | The focused control, `activate` |
| `down` of `up` / `left` | Focus moves to the previous one. `id` is the new focus, `action` is `focus` |
| `down` of `down` / `right` | Focus moves to the next one. Same as above |
| Pointer `tap` or `double_tap` | The hit control, `activate`. Focus moves to it |
| Pointer `hold` | The hit control, `long_press` |
| (2.9) `activate` on a `field` | Editing starts, `action` is `edit`. See “Text fields (2.9)” |

An `ev` that is not an event table from section 4 returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. A control does not store `selected`. The script passes it every frame. The library does not draw a pressed look. `press` only tells the script.

**Whether focus is drawn**: focus is drawn only while keys are driving it. A device with no touchscreen always draws it. A device with a touchscreen starts drawing it after a key event is given to `handle_event`, and stops drawing it after a pointer event is given to `handle_event` (the focus itself is kept, and the next key starts from it).

`double_tap` is the second tap: two quick taps on a button produce two `activate` results, and a switch is toggled twice.

## Setting focus (2.7)

```lua
ui:focus(id)          -- no return value
local id = ui:focused()
```

`focus(id)` replaces the kept focus with `id`. At the next `end_frame` it is checked like any other kept focus: if this frame has a `button`, `switch`, or (2.9) `field` with that `id`, focus stays on it; if not (or it is a `label`, `image`, `row`, or `column`), focus falls on the first one. It can be called at any time, including between `begin_frame` and `end_frame`. It draws nothing and puts nothing on screen; to see the new focus, call `ctx:invalidate()` as usual. It does not change whether focus is drawn (see above), and `handle_event` does not return `focus` because of it. An empty `id` returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`; a non-string raises a Lua error (section 0).

Until the next `end_frame`, focus is that `id`: `focused()` returns it, and `ok` produces `press` and `activate` for it; arrow keys move among the previous frame's controls, starting from the first one if `id` is not among them. After `invalidate` the host redraws before the next event (section 5), so calling it together with `invalidate` avoids this case.

`focused()` returns the kept focus `id`, or nil when there is no focus. It is nil for a newly created object and when the previous frame had no hittable control.

Usage: open another screen from a button, and on return put focus back on that button.

```lua
local screen, back_to = "home", nil

function on_input(ctx, ev)
  if ev.type == "key" and ev.key == "back" and screen ~= "home" then
    if ev.phase == "up" then
      screen = "home"
      ui:focus(back_to)          -- back to the button that opened this screen
      ctx:invalidate()
    end
    return true
  end
  local id, action = ui:handle_event(ev)
  if action == "activate" and screen == "home" then
    back_to, screen = id, id       -- the button id is the screen it opens
    ctx:invalidate()
    return true
  end
  if action then ctx:invalidate(); return true end
  return false
end
```

To return to a position several levels back, the script keeps its own table as a stack: push `focused()` when entering a screen, pop and `focus` when leaving one. Use `focus` as well to stay on a neighbouring item after deleting a list item, or to start on “Cancel” when showing a confirmation.

## Text fields (2.9)

```lua
local todo = { title = "", note = "" }

function on_draw(ctx, g)
  g:clear()
  ui:begin_frame(g)
  ui:field("title", { x = 24, y = 96, w = 432, h = 56, text = todo.title, placeholder = "What to do",
    max_chars = 24, enter = "next",
    on_change = function(ctx, text) todo.title = text; ctx:invalidate() end })
  ui:field("note", { x = 24, y = 168, w = 432, h = 120, text = todo.note, placeholder = "Note",
    multiline = true, max_chars = 200, enter = "done",
    on_change = function(ctx, text) todo.note = text; ctx:invalidate() end,
    on_end = function(ctx) ctx:invalidate() end })
  ui:button("save", { x = 24, y = 304, w = 432, h = 56, text = "Save" })
  ui:end_frame()
end

function on_input(ctx, ev)
  local id, action = ui:handle_event(ev)
  if id == "save" and action == "activate" then
    ui:stop_edit()
    save(ctx, todo)
  end
  if action then ctx:invalidate(); return true end
  return false
end
```

`field` is a hittable control. It takes its place in the focus order by when it was added, together with `button` and `switch`. It edits text with the docked input from section 4. Fields:

| Field | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `text` | The current text. The script passes it every frame; the library does not store it. Default `""` |
| `font` | The font for drawing the text when not editing. Default `ctx.fonts.medium` |
| `radius` | The corner radius of the box |
| `placeholder` `max_chars` `kind` `multiline` `enter` `on_change` `on_end` | The same as in `ctx.input:edit`. They are passed to it when editing starts |

**How it is drawn**: a stroked box (line width 1, 2 when focus is drawn). The box keeps 8 pixels of margin on each side, and `text` is drawn inside. When `kind` is `"secret"`, each character is drawn as `*`. A single line is vertically centered, with an ellipsis when it overflows. Multiple lines wrap by character from the top down, and the overflow is clipped. When `text` is empty, `placeholder` is drawn (color 8). While editing, the host redraws the text and the cursor inside the box (section 4, “Text area”).

**Starting to edit**: `activate` on a `field` (a tap, or `ok` while focus is on it) calls `ctx.input:edit` with the fields declared in the previous frame. `rect` is the area inside the box after the margin. `handle_event` returns `id, "edit"`. When editing cannot start (for example `busy`, or a value of `max_chars`, `kind`, and so on that breaks the rules), it returns `id, "activate"` as usual: `ui:field` itself checks only `x`, `y`, `w`, and `h`, and the edit options are checked only when editing starts. A wrong type (such as `multiline = "yes"`) raises a Lua error in `handle_event`. Another `activate` on the `field` being edited does not start again, and still returns `id, "edit"`. While editing, a tap inside the box moves the cursor. The host takes it and does not pass it to `handle_event`.

**Ending the edit**:

- When editing ends with the confirm key or the back key, the library first calls this field's `on_end`. When `enter` is `"next"` and the key was the confirm key, the library then starts editing the first `field` after it in the previous frame's order, focus moves there, and the keyboard stays up. With no `field` after it, editing just ends.
- While editing, `activate` on another `field` of this object ends the current edit (without calling its `on_end`) and starts editing that `field`; the keyboard stays up. If editing cannot start on that `field`, it returns `id, "activate"`, and the original edit has already ended.
- `ui:stop_edit()` ends this object's current edit, puts the keyboard away, and returns the final text. It does not call `on_end`. When nothing is being edited it returns nil.
- At `end_frame`, if the `field` being edited was not declared this frame, the library ends the edit without calling `on_end`. There is no need to put the keyboard away separately when changing screens.

`ui:editing()` returns the `id` of the `field` this object is editing, or nil when there is none.

Only one of `ctx.input:edit` called by the script and a `field` edit can be active at a time. The other returns `busy`.
